q: You are motoring east along this coast and want a three-point fix with the hand-bearing compass. Which mark do you take last?
a: B — abeam, its bearing changes fastest
o: A — fine on the bow, the easiest to see
C — on the quarter, soon out of sight
The nearest mark, whatever its bearing
why: Take marks ahead or astern first — their bearings change slowly — and the one abeam last; then note the time and log.

q: You can see these three marks but have time for only two bearings. Which pair gives the most reliable fix?
why: Two position lines cut best near 90°: A and B are about 90° apart, the other pairs cut at shallow angles.

q: You come on deck at night and find this. What do you do first?
a: Move the phone well away from the compass
o: Apply 15° of deviation from the card
Steer by the GPS COG for the night
Swing the compass at first light
why: A phone (its speaker magnet) next to the compass deflects it; remove it before you trust any heading.

fig.title: Night watch, 0230
lines: Crew's phone left beside the compass

q: Your three bearings give this cocked hat, with a reef to the south. Which point do you take as your position?
a: C — the corner nearest the reef
o: A — the corner furthest from the reef
Any corner — the triangle is small
why: Assume the worst: use the corner of the cocked hat nearest the danger and plan your next course from it.

q: You want a fix from these two radar targets. Which position lines do you plot?
o: One bearing with the other's range
The bearings, averaged with the compass
why: Radar ranges are accurate; radar bearings suffer from beam width and yaw — cross two ranges.

q: Your house batteries die on a night passage. What do you steer by now?
a: The steering compass — it needs no power
o: The handheld GPS and its COG
why: A fluxgate needs power; the magnetic steering compass does not — it is the backup for every electronic heading.

fig.title: 0400, house batteries flat
lines: Handheld GPS in the grab bag

q: This alarm sounds on a night passage. What do you do?
a: Run a DR from the 0255 fix and fix by the lights
o: Keep steering on the plotter's boat icon
Heave to until the GPS comes back
Reset the plotter and trust its next fix
why: With no satellites the icon is frozen or guessing: work by DR from the last fix and fix visually.

fig.title: Plotter alarm
lines: Lights of the coast in sight

q: This is the state of your boat in spring. What do you do before the first passage?
a: Swing the compass and make a new card
o: Keep the old card — it will be close
Add 2° to the old card on every heading
why: New magnets and electronics near the compass change its deviation: swing it and draw up a new card.

fig.title: After the winter refit
lines: Plotter moved next to the binnacle

q: Two lighthouses on this coast could be this light. How do you tell which one it is?
a: Time its period with a stopwatch and count flashes
o: Judge its brightness against the charted range
Note its colour and compare it with the chart
Wait until it is abeam, then take a bearing
why: Identify a light by its characteristic: count the flashes, time the full period, match the chart or List of Lights.

q: This is your plan for the day. How do you change the fixing routine at 1100?
a: Fix far more often — every 10 to 15 minutes
o: Keep the hourly fix — the plan is unchanged
Fix only at each waypoint on the plotter
Fix less often — you need eyes on deck
why: The closer the danger, the more often you fix: hourly in open water, every few minutes among rocks.

q: You take this bearing of a headland light with the hand-bearing compass, well clear of any steel. Which bearing do you plot?
why: Magnetic to true: subtract westerly variation — 312°M − 3°W = 309°T. Clear of steel there is no deviation.

q: You take these three bearings for a fix. Which true bearings do you plot?
why: Easterly variation is added going from magnetic to true: +4° on each bearing.

q: You steer straight down this charted transit and read the steering compass. What deviation does it have on this heading?
why: 125°T + 3°W = 128°M; the compass reads 131°C, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W (C + dev = M).
ref: Compass — checking deviation on a transit

q: You sight along this charted transit with the hand-bearing compass and read this. What does it tell you?
o: It reads 2° high — apply 2°W to bearings
It reads 2° low — apply 2°E to bearings
why: 058°T + 2°W = 060°M, exactly what the compass reads: from that spot it has no deviation.

q: The rose on your chart was printed some years ago. Which true bearing of the lighthouse goes on the chart?
You take this bearing over the steering compass. Which true bearing do you plot?
why: Deviation goes with the ship's head, not the bearing: 075°C + 4°E = 079°M; − 2°W = 077°T.

q: Your three bearings give this cocked hat, about a mile across. What do you do?
a: Check each mark's identity and retake the bearings
o: Use its centre — the errors average out
Accept it — any fix beats a DR
Plot the corner nearest your DR and go on
why: A big cocked hat means an error — a wrong mark, a misread, a slow round of bearings: check and fix again.

q: You plan a three-point fix from these marks. Which one do you leave out?
a: B — a buoy can drag or be off station
o: A — a lighthouse is too close to plot
C — a church spire is not a sea mark
None — any charted object will do
why: Use fixed, well-charted objects; a floating mark may be out of position, so it makes a poor fix mark.

q: You work up this running fix. How do you transfer the 1015 position line?
why: Move the first line by the run between bearings: log 19.4 − 14.2 = 5.2 M along the course, 090°T.

q: You allow for the tide in this running fix. By what do you move the first position line?
why: Water track 270°T 6.0 M plus tide 180°T 1.2 M gives the ground track: 6.1 M along 259°T.

q: You note the log at these two bearings of the light. How far off it are you when it comes abeam?
why: 45° on the bow, then abeam: a right isosceles triangle, so distance off abeam = run = 25.9 − 22.6 = 3.3 M.

fig.title: Bow and beam bearings
lines: Light 45° on the starboard bow, log 22.6

q: The angle of the light on your bow has doubled. What is your distance off it now?
why: Doubling the angle on the bow makes an isosceles triangle: distance off at the second bearing = run, 11.2 − 8.4 = 2.8 M.

fig.title: Doubling the angle on the bow
lines: Light 30° on the port bow, log 8.4
Light 60° on the port bow, log 11.2

q: You want a position line from the depth. Which charted depth are you over, and so which contour are you on?
why: Water depth 17.4 + 0.6 = 18.0 m; minus 3.0 m of tide = 15.0 m below chart datum: the 15 m contour.

q: You plot this fix and check the sounder, which reads from the waterline. What do you make of the fix?
a: It is suspect — fix again and check the marks
o: It stands — the sounder must be faulty
It stands — the tide explains the gap
It stands — the chart is simply out of date
why: 12.0 m − 1.5 m of tide = 10.5 m below datum, not the 27–31 m charted round the fix: the depth says the fix is wrong.

q: You are closing the coast at night. At what distance do you expect this light to rise above the horizon?
why: Geographical range 2.08 × (√36 + √2.5), heights in metres = 15.8 M; inside the 18 M nominal range, so it rises there.
ref: Position lines — rising and dipping lights

q: You hope to get a distance off as this light rises above the horizon. Will it work?
a: No — you first see it at about 12 M
o: Yes — it rises at about 17.5 M
Yes — it rises at about 14.6 M
Yes — it rises at about 18.7 M
why: 2.08 × (√49 + √2) = 17.5 M geographical, heights in metres, but the light carries only 12 M: it appears at 12 M, not on the horizon.
ref: Position lines — rising and dipping lights

q: You stand on the coachroof and watch the lighthouse dip below the horizon. How far off is it?
why: The table is 2.08 × (√H + √h) with heights in metres: a 40 m light seen from 3 m dips at 16.8 M.

fig.title: Dipping distances (M)
lines: Light 30 m: eye 2 m 14.3 · eye 3 m 15.0
Light 40 m: eye 2 m 16.1 · eye 3 m 16.8
Light 50 m: eye 2 m 17.6 · eye 3 m 18.3
You: eye 3 m, the 40 m light dips

q: You take a bearing at the moment the light rises. Where are you?
a: 13.3 M from the light, on 218°T from it
o: 13.3 M from the light, on 038°T from it
20.0 M from the light, on 218°T from it
13.3 M from the light, on 222°T from it
why: 2.08 × (√25 + √2), metres = 13.3 M; 040°M − 2°W = 038°T, so you lie on the reciprocal, 218°T from the light.
ref: Position fixing — rising light and bearing

q: You read the radar like this for a fix. Which true bearing of the headland do you plot?
why: A head-up EBL is relative to the bow: 250°M + 040° = 290°M; − 2°W = 288°T.

q: You want a radar range for a fix off this coast. Which target do you use?
o: The nearest echo, whatever it is
why: Steep cliffs give a hard echo at the water's edge; a low beach may not show, and hills lie well behind the coastline.

q: You expect this buoy on the radar screen but cannot find it. What do you do?
a: Turn sea clutter down until speckle just shows
o: Turn the gain up to maximum as well
Switch to the 12 M range for a wider view
Trust the screen — the buoy has gone
why: Too much sea-clutter suppression wipes out weak echoes close in; reduce it until a little sea speckle shows.

fig.title: Radar, 0500
lines: Sea moderate · range 1.5 M, rings 0.5 M
Red can buoy 0.4 M ahead not showing

q: How do you plot your position from these radar readings?
why: 115°M − 3°W = 112°T to the headland; you lie on the reciprocal, 292°T, 2.4 M out from it.

q: Coasting at night, you open this status page. How do you treat the GPS position?
a: As poor — check it against bearings and depth
o: As good — four satellites make a fix
As exact — HDOP only affects height
As good once it has settled for a minute
why: A high HDOP means poor satellite geometry and a wide error; cross-check with a visual fix and the sounder.

q: Your only GPS behaves like this. What is the likely cause?
a: No sky view — the antenna must be outside
o: Wrong datum — set it to ED50
Low battery — plug it into 12 V
Deviation — move it from the compass
why: GPS needs a clear view of the sky; below decks or under a sprayhood the signals fade and the fix wanders.

fig.title: Handheld GPS
lines: Kept on the chart table below

q: The GPS lat/long plots you on these rocks, yet you can see them well clear to the north-east. What is the likely cause?
a: The datum — apply the chart's shift note
o: Lag — the GPS is behind the boat
why: On a chart drawn to an older datum the stated shift must be applied to WGS84 positions, or GPS fixes plot in the wrong place.

q: You use the GPS range and bearing to this charted waypoint for a quick fix. Where do you plot yourself?
why: BRG is from you to the waypoint, so you lie on the reciprocal: 040° + 180° = 220°T, 3.2 M from it.
ref: GPS — range and bearing to a waypoint

q: You plot your fix from this waypoint, which is charted on the rock itself. Where are you?
why: 107°M − 4°W = 103°T from you to the waypoint; you lie on the reciprocal, 283°T, 4.6 M from it.

q: You are on this bearing of the light, and the sounder reads from the waterline. Where on the line are you?
a: B — where it crosses the 10 m depth
o: A — where it crosses the 20 m depth
C — where it crosses the 5 m depth
Anywhere — one bearing gives no fix
why: 13.2 m − 3.2 m of tide = 10.0 m below chart datum: the bearing crosses that depth at B.

q: Your fix and your DR disagree like this. What do you do?
a: Trust the fix and restart the plot from it
o: Trust the DR — it has three hours of log
Split the difference between the two
Ignore both and wait for the GPS
why: A good fix beats a DR; the gap is the tide you left out — start the DR again from the fix and allow for it.

fig.title: Log, 1200
lines: Three-bearing fix: 1.8 M SE of the DR

q: The visual fix and the GPS disagree. Which do you work from?
a: The visual fix — the depth agrees with it
o: The GPS — satellites beat a hand compass
A point halfway between, as a compromise
The GPS — but add 0.5 M to all clearances
why: Two independent checks agree — the bearings and the sounder; the GPS gap is likely the datum, so work from the visual fix.

fig.title: Off the Breton coast, 1530
lines: Visual three-point fix: small cocked hat
GPS position: 0.5 M west of it
Corrected sounding matches the visual fix
Chart: old survey, a datum note

q: Your crew times the light like this. Which charted light is it?
o: A — the dark gap is 12 s
A or B — the period cannot be timed
Neither — the timing fits no light
why: The period runs from the start of one group to the start of the next: 3 s + 12 s = 15 s, so Fl(3) 15s.
ref: Fixing at night — timing a light

fig.title: Stopwatch, 2315
lines: White light, groups of three flashes
Dark from end of group to next: 12 s

q: You time a light to identify it for a fix. Which charted light are you watching?
a: D — occulting, light longer than dark
o: C — isophase, light equal to dark
why: Light longer than dark is occulting; on 6 s + off 2 s = an 8 s period: Oc 8s.

fig.title: Timing a light
lines: White light: on 6 s, off 2 s, repeating

q: How often do you need a fix to keep to this plan?
why: 0.5 M at 6 kn takes 0.5 ÷ 6 = 0.083 h = 5 minutes, so fix at least every 5 minutes.

fig.title: Inshore passage at night
lines: Rocks 0.5 M either side of the track
Plan: never run more than 0.5 M unfixed

q: Your crew asks why the deviation on this card changes as you change course. What do you tell them?
a: The boat's iron and wiring turn with her
o: Magnetic north shifts as the course changes
The compass card lags behind in a turn
The card is wrong — deviation is fixed
why: Deviation comes from the boat's own magnetism — engine, keel bolts, wiring — which swings round the compass with each heading.

q: You swing the compass by sighting a transit over it on each heading. Which deviation do you write down for 090°C?
why: On 090°C the transit reads 200°C against 202°M: the compass reads 2° low, so deviation is 2°E.

q: You need a hand-bearing compass fix. Where do you stand to take the bearings?
why: A hand-bearing compass picks up deviation near steel, engines and speakers: use it in the open, clear of them.

fig.title: Where to stand
lines: A: beside the steering compass pedestal
B: on the side deck, clear of fittings
C: in the hatch, right over the engine
D: under the sprayhood, by the speakers

q: Something is wrong with the heading. What do you suspect first?
a: The kedge is deflecting the compass
o: The tide is setting you 12° east
The GPS has lost its datum
why: A steel anchor or tool near the compass adds deviation of its own; move it and check the heading again.

fig.title: Day passage, 1100
lines: GPS COG 168°M, no tide, no leeway
Steel kedge stowed under the binnacle at 1000

q: You need this fix on the chart quickly and without slips. How do you plot it?
a: Range and bearing from the waypoint
o: Lat and long, with dividers on both scales
A photo of the plotter screen instead
Wait to plot it until the sea calms
why: From a charted waypoint the fix is one line and one distance — quicker, with fewer slips, than lat/long in a seaway.

fig.title: Plotting the GPS fix
lines: Boat motion lively at the chart table

q: How much do you trust this running fix?
a: Only as far as the run between the bearings
o: As much as a three-point fix
More than two bearings taken at once
Fully — the light is a fixed point
why: A running fix carries every error of course, log and tide over the run: the longer the run, the poorer the fix.

fig.title: Running fix, 2 h between bearings
lines: Tidal stream taken from a diamond
Course held only to ±5° in the swell
Log known to under-read a little

q: You altered course between the two bearings. How do you transfer the 2200 position line?
why: Add the legs as vectors: 1.5 M on 000°T then 2.0 M on 060°T give a resultant of 3.0 M along 035°T.

fig.title: Running fix with a course change

q: You take these bearings with the hand-bearing compass from the foredeck, clear of all steel. Which true bearings do you plot?
why: The deviation card belongs to the steering compass, not to a hand compass used clear of steel: apply only the 2°W variation.

fig.title: Three-point fix, 1615
lines: Steering compass card: 3°E on this heading

q: You check the hand-bearing compass on a transit from the cockpit, then take a fix from the same spot without altering course. Which true bearings do you plot?
why: 145°T + 3°W = 148°M, the compass reads 151°: 3° high. Same spot, same heading: −3° deviation, then −3°W variation.
ref: Hand-bearing compass — deviation found on a transit

fig.title: Hand compass check, cockpit
lines: Hand compass on the transit reads 151°

q: You hear this foghorn and want a position line from it. Can you use it?
a: No — sound gives no reliable bearing in fog
o: Yes — take a hand bearing of the sound
Yes — its loudness gives the distance
Yes — cross its bearing with the sounder
why: Fog bends and blanks sound: the direction and loudness of a fog signal are no guide to its bearing or range.

fig.title: Fog, 0700
lines: Foghorn heard, seemingly on the port bow

q: In fog you run a line of soundings east, one every 0.5 M; the sounder reads from the waterline. Which track have you been on?
why: Reduce each sounding to chart datum: 21, 17, 12, 9 m − 3.0 m of tide = 18, 14, 9, 6 m — the pattern charted along A.
ref: Fixing in fog — a line of soundings

q: On a night passage you find the plotter like this. Where do you start your DR from?
o: The plotter's boat icon where it is now
The next waypoint on the route
why: With no fix the plotter only extrapolates its last COG and SOG; the last fix you can trust is the one in the log book.

fig.title: Plotter, 0340
lines: Boat icon still moving on the last COG/SOG

q: Between these two bearings you sail two legs with the stream setting you SSW. By what do you move the 0900 position line?
why: Add both legs and the hour's tide: 3.0 M on 090°T + 3.0 M on 140°T + 1.0 M on 200°T = 5.6 M along 125°T.
ref: Running fix — course change and tide

q: Your bearings are an hour and a half apart, and the stream changes in that time. How do you move the 0800 position line?
why: 7.5 M on 045°T, then the tide hour by hour: 1.2 M + 1.0 M (half an hour at 2.0 kn) on 090°T = 9.2 M along 055°T.
ref: Running fix — tide hour by hour

fig.title: Running fix, 0800–0930
lines: Bearings of the light at 0800 and 0930

q: Out of sight of land, you steer straight at the setting sun to check the steering compass. What is its deviation on this heading?
why: Sun 292°T + 2°W = 294°M; the compass reads 297°, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W (C + dev = M).

q: You check the steering compass on a transit on four headings and get this. What does it point to?
a: The compass is mounted out of line with the keel
o: Steel gear stowed close to the binnacle
A normal deviation curve for a yacht
A compass card that sticks in its bowl
why: Iron gives a deviation that changes with the heading; the same error on every heading is a lubber line set off the fore-and-aft line.

q: Your chart has two compass roses, both corrected to this year. You take a hand bearing of the light. Which true bearing do you plot?
why: Variation changes across a chart: use the rose nearest you, 2°W here — 060°M − 2° = 058°T.

q: Your chart has two roses printed some years ago. You are close to the east one. Which true bearing of the light do you plot?
ref: Variation — annual change and the nearest rose

q: You close the coast at low water, waiting for this light to rise. At what distance do you expect it?
why: At low water the light stands 30 + (5.0 − 1.0) = 34 m above the sea: 2.08 × (√34 + √2.5) = 15.4 M.
ref: Rising lights — height of tide on the light

fig.title: Light list and tide
lines: Light Fl 10s, 30 m above MHWS, 20 M
MHWS 5.0 m · height of tide now 1.0 m

q: You bob your head to check the light: standing you see it, sitting you do not. How far off is it?
why: Just under one horizon, just over the other: 2.08 × (√45 + √1.5) = 16.5 M and 2.08 × (√45 + √3) = 17.6 M.
ref: Rising and dipping lights — bobbing a light

fig.title: Bobbing the light, 2240
lines: Standing, eye 3.0 m: light just in sight
Sitting, eye 1.5 m: light below the horizon

q: You close this low coast at night on radar. How far off the beach are you?
a: About 2.2 M — the echo is the hills
o: About 5.2 M — the echo is the beach
About 8.2 M — add the hills' 3.0 M
About 3.7 M — halfway, to be safe
why: Low dunes give little echo; the first strong one is the high ground behind: 5.2 − 3.0 = 2.2 M to the beach.

q: You want a radar range on this low island as soon as it appears. At about what range do you expect its first echo?
why: Radar horizon: 2.2 × (√4 + √5) = 2.2 × 4.24 ≈ 9.3 M; a low target shows only when it is above that horizon.
ref: Radar — range of a low target

fig.title: Radar on passage
lines: Low island, 5 m high, no cliffs

q: You need the headland on radar for a fix. Which control do you adjust?
o: The range, to a longer scale
why: Rain clutter (FTC) breaks up the blotch of a shower so the solid echo of the land shows through it.

fig.title: Radar, 0300
lines: Rain squall between you and the headland
Headland echo lost in a blotch of rain

q: The radar ranges of A and B cross at two points; the sounder reads from the waterline. Which is your position?
o: Y — it is nearer the coast
why: Two range circles cut twice; the depth decides: 31 m − 2.0 m of tide = 29 m below datum, as charted at X.

q: You measure the range of this headland for a fix. Where on its echo do you set the VRM?
o: On the middle of the echo
why: The near edge of an echo is the coastline facing you; the echo's depth is the beam and pulse length smearing it outwards.

fig.title: Radar, 3 M scale, rings 0.5 M
lines: Headland echo: a thick band 0.2 M deep

q: You can just see one headland through the haze. Which pair of position lines gives the best fix on it?
a: Radar range and a hand bearing of it
o: Radar bearing and a hand bearing of it
Radar range and a radar bearing of it
Radar bearings of its two edges
why: Each source at its best: the radar's accurate range crossed with a visual compass bearing, cutting at 90°.
ref: Radar — range with a visual bearing

fig.title: Haze, 1500
lines: One headland in sight, about 2.5 M off

q: You fix by these three lights at night. In which order do you take the bearings?
why: Ahead or astern first — their bearings change slowly — and the light nearest the beam last, as its bearing changes fastest.

fig.title: Night fix, three lights
lines: A: broad on the starboard quarter
B: fine on the port bow

q: Only these two marks are in sight, one ahead and one astern. How good is a fix from their bearings?
a: Poor — the lines cut at a fine angle
o: Good — the marks lie on opposite sides
Good — both marks are well charted
Good — if both are taken quickly
why: Bearings ahead and astern are nearly one line: they hold you on track but say little about how far along it you are.

q: As the front and rear beacons come in line, you take one compass bearing for a fix. Which mark do you choose?
a: C — it cuts the transit near 90°
o: D — it lies closest to the transit
E — it lies on the other side of it
Any — the transit is exact anyway
why: A transit is a perfect position line without a compass; cross it with the bearing that cuts it nearest 90°.
ref: Position fixing — a transit and a bearing

q: Your new fix disagrees with both the EP and the sounder. What do you make of it?
a: Doubt the fix — check each mark's identity
o: Trust the fix — the cocked hat is tiny
Average the fix and the EP
Trust the fix — the sounder has seen fish
why: A tiny cocked hat only means the bearings agree; when depth and EP both disagree, a misidentified mark is the likely cause.

fig.title: Log, 1940
lines: EP with tide: 1.5 M north of the fix
Chart: 25 m at the fix, 9 m at the EP

q: Your 1200 fix lands away from the DR like this. What tidal stream have you had since 1000?
why: The DR left the tide out, so the gap from DR to fix is the tide: 2.0 M towards 045°T in 2 hours = 1.0 kn.

fig.title: Log, 1000–1200
lines: 1200: DR by log and course, no tide
1200: fix lies 2.0 M on 045°T from the DR

q: You have two bearings of the same light, an hour apart. Which line do you move for the running fix, and which way?
a: The first, forward along the ground track
o: The second, back along the course steered
The first, along the bearing of the light
The second, forward along the ground track
why: Carry the earlier position line forward by the distance and direction made good over the ground; cross it with the later one.

fig.title: Running fix
lines: Ground track and run known for the hour

q: You work a running fix under sail with this leeway. How do you transfer the 1300 position line?
why: The wind on the starboard side pushes you to port: water track 250° − 5° = 245°T; run 24.0 − 20.0 = 4.0 M.

q: You use the bow-and-beam bearings of this light with a foul tide. How far off it are you when it is abeam?
why: Distance off abeam equals the run over the ground, not the log: 14.0 − 10.0 = 4.0 M less 1.0 M of foul tide = 3.0 M.
ref: Running fix — bow and beam with tide

fig.title: Bow and beam bearings
lines: Light 45° on the starboard bow, log 10.0
Foul tide dead on the bow, 1.0 kn

q: Your crew puts 28 m into the dipping formula for this light. Which height should go in?
why: Charted light heights are above MHWS; with the tide 5.0 m below it the light stands 28 + 6.0 − 1.0 = 33 m above the sea.

q: This light suddenly appears ahead. Can you take the moment as its rising distance?
a: No — it came out of the haze, not over the horizon
o: Yes — it rises at 16.1 M from your height of eye
Yes — every light first shows at its horizon
Yes — but take off the 6 M of visibility
why: A rising distance needs a clear night; in 6 M haze the light shows when you close the haze, well inside its 16.1 M horizon.

q: You see this on a clear night. Can you take a rising distance now?
a: Not yet — wait for the light itself to show
o: Yes — the loom marks its geographical range
Yes — add 2 M to the rising distance
Yes — the loom's brightness gives the range
why: The loom is the beam lighting the sky above the horizon; the rising distance applies only when the light itself appears.

fig.title: Clear night, 0200
lines: A glow sweeps the sky beyond the horizon
Every 10 s, where the Fl 10s light lies
The light itself not yet in sight

q: Two ways of plotting the same GPS reading disagree like this. What is the likely cause?
a: The waypoint was mistyped — check it on the chart
o: The GPS has just lost its fix
The chart is on an older datum
The GPS is set to magnetic bearings
why: A range and bearing is only as good as the waypoint: if lat/long plots fine, check the stored waypoint against the chart.
ref: GPS — range and bearing to a waypoint

fig.title: GPS check, 1120
lines: Lat/long fix: at sea, close to your EP
WP 'Bec' typed in by hand last winter

q: Your GPS has died on a night passage and only one light is in sight. How do you fix your position?
a: A running fix: two bearings an hour apart
o: One bearing of it, plotted as a fix
Its brightness against the nominal range
None — keep the DR until daylight
why: One light gives one position line at a time; transfer the first by the run and tide and cross it with the second.
ref: GPS failure — a running fix at night

fig.title: Night passage, 0130
lines: No other lights above the horizon
Steady course, tide from the atlas

q: You read this on a night passage. How do you navigate until 0600?
a: On visual fixes and DR; the GPS is suspect
o: On the GPS — its track is smooth and steady
On the GPS, shifted 3 M to match the fix
On the AIS positions of ships around you
why: Interference can give a smooth but false GPS track; AIS uses the same satellites. Fix by bearings, depth and DR.

fig.title: NAVTEX, 2300
lines: GPS track smooth, 3 M off the visual fix
AIS targets jumping about on the plotter

q: Your GPS failed an hour ago and you want to identify the first light you see. Which of these should be in sight now?
o: A — its range is the longer
Both — each is inside its nominal range
Neither — both are below your horizon
ref: Rising lights — identifying a landfall light

fig.title: EP 0300, GPS failed
lines: Light A: 60 m, 25 M · 22 M off by EP
Light B: 20 m, 15 M · 12 M off by EP

q: You see this light ahead, and two charted lights share its characteristic. Which one is it?
a: A — B is far beyond its range
o: B — it is the brighter of the two
Either — time it again to be sure
why: Use the EP: B lies 30 M off, well beyond its 18 M range, so the Fl(2) 10s in sight must be A at 10 M.
ref: Fixing at night — identifying a light

fig.note: EP: light A 10 M, light B 30 M; both Fl(2) 10s 18 M

q: You cross this stream near the rocks. How often do you fix to keep to your rule?
why: Halfway to the rocks is 0.5 M; at 2.0 kn the stream sets you that far in 0.5 ÷ 2.0 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes.

fig.title: Cross-tide passage
lines: Rocks 1.0 M down-tide of your track
Rule: fix before it can set you halfway

q: You find this when checking the steering compass on a transit. What is the cause?
a: Current in the cables beside the compass
o: Heat from the engine bay below
why: A wire carrying current makes its own magnetic field; run cables in twisted pairs, well clear of the compass.

fig.title: Transit check, same heading
lines: Engine off: compass agrees with the transit
Charging cables run under the binnacle

q: Your crew leaves these by the binnacle on watch. Which one can stay there?
why: Aluminium is not magnetic; steel, speaker magnets and steel-cased batteries all deflect a compass close by.

q: Your new fluxgate compass shows this message. What do you do?
a: Motor slow full circles, as the manual says
o: Copy the steering compass deviation card
Nothing — a fluxgate needs no calibration
why: A fluxgate corrects its own deviation once it has been swung: slow, steady turns in calm water while it measures.

fig.title: After the refit
lines: New fluxgate compass for the autopilot
Calm sea, open water, no traffic

q: You take a bearing over the steering compass on a heading between the card's entries. Which true bearing do you plot?
why: Interpolate for the ship's head: 060°C lies a third of the way from 2°E to 4°E ≈ 3°E; 300° + 3° − 1° = 302°T.

q: You leave harbour with these leading marks dead astern and read the steering compass. What is its deviation on this heading?
why: Marks astern on 340°T put your heading on 160°T; + 2°W = 162°M; the compass reads 165°, 3° high, so 3°W.
ref: Compass — checking on a transit astern

q: You doubt the steering compass in mid-Channel, out of sight of land. How can you check it?
a: Steer at the setting sun and compare its tabled bearing
o: Compare it with the GPS COG, tide and all
Compare it with the hand compass at the chart table
Wait for a charted transit tomorrow
why: The sun's true bearing at rising or setting comes from tables: point the bow at it and compare with the compass.

fig.title: Mid-Channel, 1840
lines: Steering compass looks a few degrees off

q: In fog the plotter and the radar disagree about the headland. What do you do?
a: Trust the radar and the depth: stand off now
o: Trust the plotter: radar ranges are poor
Split the difference: call it 0.8 M
Trust the plotter until the fog lifts
why: The radar range and the sounder agree, the plotter stands alone — a chart offset or a bad fix. Open the distance.
ref: Fixing in fog — radar and plotter

fig.title: Fog, visibility 0.1 M
lines: Radar VRM on the headland: 0.6 M
Sounder: the depth charted 0.6 M off

q: You take a three-point fix in the usual order. When do you note the time and log?
a: As you take the last bearing
o: Before you take the first bearing
Once the fix is on the chart
why: The abeam bearing, taken last, changes fastest, so the fix belongs to that moment: note time and log as you take it.

fig.title: Three-point fix
lines: Time and log go in the log book

q: You check the steering compass on a transit, upright and heeled, on the same heading. What explains these readings?
a: Heeling error — the boat's iron tilts round the compass
o: Variation that changes with the tack
Leeway, which differs on each tack
A compass card sticking when heeled
why: Heeled, the boat's iron moves relative to the gimballed compass, so deviation changes with the heel and the tack.

q: Your crew took the beam mark first and finished the round of bearings at 1404. How far did you move during the round?
why: 7.5 kn × 4/60 h = 0.5 M; the beam bearing, taken first, is half a mile stale — take the mark nearest the beam last.

q: Light A has dropped out of sight before your second bearing. Can you still get a running fix?
a: Yes — A's line moved 6.0 M along 090°T, crossed with B's
o: No — both bearings must be of one mark
Yes — A's line moved 6.0 M along 030°T, crossed with B's
Yes — A's and B's lines crossed as taken
why: Any position line can be transferred: move A's line by the run, 16.0 − 10.0 = 6.0 M along the track, and cross it with B's.

fig.title: Running fix, night
lines: 1100: A out of sight; light B 300°T, log 16.0

q: You take one bearing over the steering compass and two with the hand compass on the foredeck. Which true bearings do you plot?
why: Only the steering compass bearing takes the card's 4°E for the ship's head: 020° + 4° − 2° = 022°T; the hand bearings take only −2°W.

q: You pass between rocks at night with these two ways of fixing. Which do you rely on?
a: B — no run and no tide to guess
o: A — one light, so no misidentification
why: A 2-hour running fix carries the errors of course, log and tide; two lights at once at 40° are fresh and need no guesses.

fig.title: Inshore at night
lines: Rocks 1 M either side of the track
A: running fix on one light, 2 h run
B: two lights at once, cut at 40°
Tide for A taken from a diamond

q: You choose a mark for a hand bearing. Which gives the more reliable bearing?
a: A — a sharp point, charted exactly
o: B — it is bigger and easier to see
B — it is nearer, so less error
why: A bearing needs a point you can pin down: the edge of a sloping headland moves with distance and the state of tide.

fig.title: Marks for a fix
lines: A: lighthouse on a rock, 4 M off
B: edge of a low, sloping headland, 2 M off
